Our June GVWG meeting was a live, online, interactive demo by Cindy Drozda and I, for one, thoroughly enjoyed it. Cindy did a fantastic job of presenting her demonstration AND simultaneously managing the multiple
cameras and all the other various A/V technology she showed off after the presentation. I’ve participated in a
few other Interactive Remote Demonstrations, or IRD’s as they are known, using similar, relatively inexpensive technology. I enjoyed them all and learned lots from all of them. I really think it is the next best thing to an
in-person demo compared to DVD’s or YouTube videos. I also believe this is going to become the new normal
for demonstrations for the next while.
Many well-known demonstrators are offering IRDs to clubs for a reasonable cost. Some of are also offering
regular IRD’s to individuals for extremely reasonable fees; cheaper than a movie in most cases. We have a few
of them listed on the Events page on the Guild website ( www.gvwg.ca ) but there are others if you Google
online woodturning demonstrations.
Speaking of online demos, I hope you all had a chance to tune in to the AAW Virtual Symposium. It was 3
days of great demonstrations and panel discussions - at a bargain price! All of the demonstrations were very
professionally done and extremely engaging and I hope the AAW continues with these types of symposia in the
future for those that are unable to attend in person.
We are continuing with our Thursday 7pm Dessert Chat sessions on Zoom. These are just social chit-chat sessions with no agenda other than to socialize, talk shop or ask questions. It is the same Zoom login credentials
every week and we are usually pretty good at getting an email out every week with the login information.
Please join us whenever you can and, of course, it is canceled on the 4th Thursday of each month in lieu of our
regular meeting.
Also, to keep things simple, our Tech Talk discussion group is now held as a separate Zoom meeting at 7:00
PM on the Monday evening following our monthly meetings. Links will be emailed to all members ahead of
time.
Please remember to try to take a photo of your Instant Gallery or President’s Challenge pieces so we can include them in our newsletter. They don’t have to be professional photos, just do the best with what you have
available. Please email your photos to editor@gvwg.ca. The photos are also great for showing your work during the meeting.
I’ve had a few reports of members not getting emails from the guild, or only some emails. In most cases the
emails were received but filed in unexpected places by their email program. Gmail is bad for that (check your
Promotions tab or Spam folder). It is also possible that we might have an incorrect email address for you. If
you are a paid-up member and you’re not getting regular emails from the guild, let me know and we’ll try to
help figure out why. You can email me at president@gvwg.ca.
Just for a little fun, and to stimulate your creativity and imagination, I’m announcing September’s President’s
Challenge early so that you have lots of time to plan and create. The September President’s Challenge is a 2x4
Challenge: Turn Something From a 2x4. It can be anything that is completely turned from all or part of a single 8-foot construction grade 2x4. It can be simple; it can be elaborate. It can be practical; it can be outlandish.
It can be silly; it can be serious. It’s not a contest so have fun with it! (Marco, Art, Steve H. – I expect to see
something from you guys!)
By Steve Fairbairn
President's Column

August Update:
It’s been so great to finally see some sunny, summer weather and to actually be able to complain, for a change,
about it being too hot! We were able to enjoy a couple weeks of the great weather at our off-grid cottage in
Howe Sound surrounded by water on one side and a mixed forest of large Red Cedar and Big Leaf Maple trees
on the other. Many of the maples have clusters of huge burls on them, but it seems that the ones that come
down during the winter storms never seem to be the ones with burls. (sigh) Our cottage community is quick to
snag the fallen trees and drag them to a central location where they can be bucked up and split for firewood.
Sadly, I never seem to be around when that happens. By the time I get to the pile, any of the beautifully figured logs have already been split into firewood. Many is the time I’ve dragged home highly figured firewood
to see what I can turn from it! I’m hatching a plan to teach my neighbors to recognize the figured rounds and
then put a bounty on them.
Every now and then I like to experiment with offset and eccentric turning so I found Steve Hansen’s presentation at our July meeting to be most interesting. As well as being a very creative turner, Steve is known for both
his and ingenuity and frugality. He demonstrated those traits once again with his presentation on how to modify your scroll chuck easily, safely, and temporarily to function as an offset chuck. Why invest the money to
buy or time to fabricate an offset chuck for the occasional foray into offset turning when, if 10 minutes, you
can modify your existing chuck? The shop tour following his presentation was another testament to his ingenuity and resourcefulness.
I look forward to seeing all of you at our August meeting. Joe Fleming will be providing us with our main
presentation. Joe is a woodturner located in San Diego who is known for his airbrushed turnings. Joe will be
giving us a recap and review of the day-long demo and 2-day class that he provided during his visit to our guild
in December 2018. If you attended his demo and/or class, or would like an introduction to airbrushing
woodturnings, or just want to learn some new tips and tricks, I urge you to attend the August meeting via
Zoom. I was very fortunate to be able to attend his class. Like many of us, I had an airbrush that I had purchased some time before but had never really gotten around to learning to use. I learned so much during those
3 days that I now have a special spot for an airbrush station next to my lathe.
If you have not been attending our online meetings, for whatever reason, I urge you to rejoin our meetings.
We miss you! We have a lot of great presentations lined up and are committed to continue providing quality,
engaging presentations from our members and, every other month, well known, internationally located turners.
If you’re unfamiliar with or uncomfortable using Zoom to attend meetings then please contact me at president@gvwg.ca and I will ensure that you receive some assistance and coaching to help get you online and comfortable using the technology, regardless of what sort of device you have available to you.
Stay well,
Steve

By Bruce Campbell
Editor's Notes
It is with some sadness that I confirm that Robert Carlson, my long-time partner in producing our
newsletter is stepping back due to other demands on his time. Robert has been the publisher o our
newsletter which means he took all the content that I and others produce and massaged it into the
beautiful layout that you have enjoyed for the last five years. I can’t say enough about the patience,
creativity, and thoughtfulness that Robert has brought to the task and quite frankly, I have not had to
worry about that side of things at all.
So, thank you Robert. You did good work.
But every coin has two sides so I would like to welcome Steve Fairbairn to the role of publisher
starting this issue. We all know Steve as our current President who has been navigating the Guild
through the troubled waters of COVID-19 and all that entails. Please join me in thanking and supporting Steve as he takes up his additional job as newsletter publisher.
The pandemic has been hard on all of us and for a variety of reasons. As far as the Guild is concerned it could have wiped us out completely had it not been for our creative Board. By adopting
remote meetings, deciding to continue through the summer, putting Tech Talk on a different night
than the on-line meeting, hosting Thursday social chats, and proactively embracing remote demonstrations, we have continued to operate in spite of the shutdown of our regular meetings. And, there
have been some upsides, too. Past members and associate members that are out-of-town have
showed up to our various meetings from California, Edmonton, Saskatoon, on other locations. It is
easier for our Board members to meet on-line rather than driving out to Port Moody as has been
done for years.
So things have changed but we are still here. As the Fall comes upon us we may still not be able to
meet at Sapperton Hall but we can still get together on-line, share information, get questions answered, be inspired by our fellow members, and have fun.
Please continue to be active members of the Guild by joining in the remote sessions. The by-line
that seems to be most appropriate is: Together we will get through this.
Stay Calm. Be Kind. Stay Safe.
Bruce Campbell Steve Fairbairn

Tech Talk continues to be held at 7:00 PM on the
Monday evening following our Guild Zoom meeting. We will stay with this arrangement as long as
we are ZOOM-ing rather than meeting at Sapperton
Hall. As usual, a link to the session will be emailed
to all members. Please join in and bring along your
question and share you experiences.
Misalignment Barry reported an interesting problem with his Oneway 1640 lathe. He noticed that
his headstock and tailstock centers did not align
when he locked his tailstock down. This causes
annoying problems when doing precision projects.
He shimmed one side of his tailstock clamp block
and was able to correct the problem but remains
concerned that the shim may wear or get pulled off.
If that should happen, several folks suggested JB
Weld epoxy putty for a more permanent solution.
Holding Spheres Larry told us about a fix he did
with Cole Jaws to make a better holding mechanism when he turns large spheres. He uses heavy
angle brackets bolters to each of the Cole jaws and
mounts wooden block to them. This makes the
equivalent of wooden jays that can then be shaped
(if needed) to hold the sphere.
During the discussion that arose Larry clarified that
he uses a heavier chuck (Stronghold in is case) with
thicker Cole jaws and this reduces flexing in the
jaws and leads to a more secure setup.
About CA Glue Mark asked is anyone had experience with Gorilla brand CA glue. The general consensus was that unless you are using a special CA
(e.g. slow-setting, rubber, coloured, etc.) then all
brands are pretty much alike. Several people pointed out that keeping unopened bottles of glue in the
freezer helps to extend their shelf life and several
pointed out that the cap should be left off of CA
glue stored at room temperature.
Bruce reported that thin CA glue can be used as a
“thinner” for thicker CA glues that have started to
stiffen up. Just squirt thin CA I the bottle of overly
thick glue and give it a good shake. .
Extending the life of sanding pads Gary found
that removing sanding discs from the sanding pad
was tearing up the pads and shortening the useful
life of his abrasives. To solve this problem, he
made a different sanding pad for each grit. He
writes:
I was tired of ruining expensive Velcro disks when pulling them off the
sanding pad. I saw a YouTube video
on how to make your own sanding
pads. They are held in an magnetic
screwdriver holder, so I can change
grits very quickly without ripping of
the Velcro backing. I now only change
the sanding disk when the sanding
disk is totally worn out rather than
every time I change grits.
A block is turned to a 2” or 3” circle,
and a hole is drilled a bit smaller than a
Cheap knock-off screwdriver bit. With
the lathe off press the screwdriver bit
into the drilled hole. Shape the block to
a taper, use foam from a kneeling pad
(Dollar Store stuff), and hot glue onto
the top of your tapered pieces. Mount
this in the lathe by the screwdriver bit
and shape the pad with a gouge or
skew. Finally, glue on Velcro strips

(again from a Dollar Store) and you
have an inexpensive sanding pad.
Make one for each grit you use when
power sanding and you are ready to

Revamping Battery Packs Des asked if
there was anything that could be done about a
battery pack that would no longer take a
charge. I found a whimsical article online
about this very topic that suggests how to
“jump start” your battery to get it back in service. The article can be found here:
https://www.theartofdoingstuff.com/batterythat-wont-recharge/
But, eventually the cells in any battery pack
will simply die. You can buy the individual
cells and replace them in you battery pack but
you will have to crack the unit open, remove
the old cells and solder new ones in place.
Steve F suggested that you avoid buying really cheap cells. They are not worth the money.
Larry suggested to check if the ends of the
cells are stainless steel or just coated. Stainless ones are much harder to solder in place.
If doing all this is not you cup of tea try visiting a remote control model shop. Most modern model units are now electric (remember
the old gas units) and these guys repair battery
packs all the time. The last time I had it done
it cost about half of the price of a new pack.
New Cyclonic Separator Steve F reports the
new purchase of a cyclonic separator from
Busy Bee.
https://www.busybeetools.com/products/
super-dust-deputy-deluxe-4in-oneida.html
The unit is quite compact with a 15 gallon
barrel that Steve hopes will be much easier to
empty than the 45 gallon one he has now.
Brue wanted to know if there was any noticeable change in airflow with the new unit and Steve will report back to us when he has it installed and tested.
Bruce reported a noticeable increase in air flow
in his dust collector system since changing
from a bag to a canister filter.
Steve H had a collection of innovative ideas for
us this month.
V-arm fine adjuster: Essentially is just a bolt
threaded through the Wolverine back stop and
is used to adjust the angle of contact on your
grinding wheel.
Flex arrester: This implement reduces the
downward deflection of your cutting end when
hollowing. It consists of a vertical pole attached to the handle end of your boring system.
At the top of the pole is an articulating caster
which rides on a large metal plate affixed to
Page 6
GVWG

the ceiling. It works extremely well.
Fingernail Jig Holster: This jig does two things.
It holds your vari-grind, or like jig, in a holster that
is strategically placed and oriented next to your
grinding wheel. In tandem with the holster is the
depth gauge. To use, insert the chisel into the holstered jig and align with the included depth gauge.
After each grind, place the held tool and vari-grind
back in the holster, loosen your capture screw and
withdraw the tool.
Bevel viewing mirror: this clever setup is very
simple and very handy. It is simply a mirror that
lets you see your bevel from the side when getting
ready to sharpen. The V-arm can be moved back
and forth until you see the bevel match the grinding wheel. Used in conjunction with Steve’s adjusting knob, this virtually eliminated the guesswork from bevel setup.
Page 7
GVWG

Sharpening Station: A pic of my sharpening
station. A slow speed 1 HP unit, with two
CBN wheels, coarse and fine. Also, a 1/2HP
unit with a blue wheel and neoprene abrasive
wheel - this units rotates BACKWARDS so
that the rubber wheel cannot catch the edge
of the chisel and kick-back.
By Steve Fairbairn

By Bruce Campbell
Cindy Drozda Demonstration - Triangular
Box
Last month we had our first remote demonstration from
well-known Colorado-based turner, Cindy Drozda.
Cindy is perhaps best known for her exquisite finals
that decorate many of her boxes and vessels. To get a
good overview of her work please visit her website at:
http://cindydrozda.com/html/Gallery.html
The project Cindy demonstrated was a triangular box.
It is an elegant project requiring careful setup on the
blank and then careful mounting and cutting on the
lathe. Details of the process are beyond the scope of
this article but Cindy did send us excellent layout documents that show how to proceed. They are shown below.
Beyond the demonstration itself, Cindy also gave us a
tour of her presentation setup and showed us her personal modifications to allow her to control the video
feed with as much expertise as her turning.
Cindy runs live demonstrations on a regular basis. The
cost is quite reasonable and is payable on-line. She
then sends you the credentials for the meeting (hosted
via ZOOM). A schedule of her demos can be found on
her website:
http://cindydrozda.com/html/Demo.html
Many thanks for Cindy for her gracious hosting and her
impressive demonstration.

Preparation Instructions
For the participants ot Cindy Drozda Signature Workshops
Subject: Triangle Box
Workshop Goals:
My main goal for all of my workshops is to help members of the Woodturning community to become
better woodturners and artists. | do this through sharing the methods, techniques, and design philosophy
that| use in my own work.
Another goal is to give participants the experience with me that they are looking for. For many, that is to
take home a piece of my signature work that they have made.
You are to be congratulated for your willingness to learn from me! It is through exposure to other tumers
that we all share and grow, as individuals and as a group. ‘Your tuming and artwork will improve as a
result, no matter what your tuming experience level at the moment.
| attend other turners’ workshops
whenever | can.
| always benefit from leaming different ideas and ways of doing things.
This is your opportunity to step into my shoes, and experience the ways that | do my work. Everyone
does things differently, and you may or may not decide to incorporate my ideas and methods into your
own work. Having exposed yourself to new methods, processes, and philosophies will make you a better
turner. You will have more options and more “tools” available for doing your own work.
Subject:
The subject of this workshop will be my “Triangle Box”.
It is a lidded container with an over-titting lid. The
outside is turned on 3 sets of centers, making it look like a triangular shape.
In addition to the steps and processes involved in the project, participants will leam boxmaking
techniques, fitting parts together, jam-fitting techniques, and multi-axis turning.

Cindy Drozda
Depending on the length of the class, we may decide to do an inlay in the top of the lid.
In a single day Triangle Box Workshop, we will all complete a Triangle Box. Multi-day Multi-Axis Box
Workshops will include other projects also.
Class Structure:
My workshops consist of short demonstrations of each step in the project, followed by time for the
participants to complete that step.
The focus will be on completing the process as a group, and learning some techniques along the way. |
do not recommend spending a lot of time sanding and finishing.
We will have a morning session, a lunch break of about 1 hour, and an afternoon session. At the end of
the day, we will leave the shop as clean as we found it. Hours of class will vary, depending on the
facility that we are using. Usually, we spend a 6-7 hour day working at the lathe.
Please contact your club’s representative for the hours of your class, and any other specific details.
Turning Experience Required:
This workshop is the lesson, not the final exam! ‘Your performance in class will not be graded or judged.
We all learn at our own level and our own rate. It is the nature of clubs and guilds that the workshop
participants will be at different levels. It's my job as instructor to challenge everyone at their level. All skill
levels are welcome, though some turning experience is highly recommended.
Technical Preparation:
You should be “current® with your own tools and methods. In other words, it will be better for you if you
have turned something recently and are reasonably comfortable with what you currently do.
You don't need excessive practice, or instruction, to prepare for this workshop. The best time to
schedule time in your shop to practice is in the weeks following the class, when you can put into action
the ideas and methods that you learned, and make them your own.
What to Bring to Class:
1 — Safety eyewear, face shield, or goggles. This is important. Eyeglasses don’t count unless they have
protective side shields and ANSI spec safety lenses.
2 - You do not need to bring wood. All of the wood will be provided.
3— Tools (list below) and any sharpening jigs that you like to use.
4— Sandpaper and finishing materials if you intend to finish your propect.

By Bruce Campbell
It’s The Little Things
A topic that has come up several times at our
Thursday Dessert Talks has been that spending
more time in the garage/shop/studio has caused
us to “fix” little things that have been put off.
Steve F set up an overhead rack to suspend tools
on retractable cords so they are out of the way but
still in easy reach. Steve H did a thorough cleanup of his wood shed and other things (see Tech
Talk). I added a bank of LED lights over my
lathe, made a permanent spot to store a small decorating tool, and glued a missing spring clip to
my sandpaper rack it had been missing for several years.
We all have a list of “little things” that we tolerate rather than “fixing”. Yet once they are
crossed off the ToDo list we get more benefit
than just the fix. We also get to release that task
from our mind. Consider your own list and how
much time you spend just thinking about it and
how you need to do that little work-around over
and over. How would it feel to have some of that
time to think/do creative things instead?
Try a little experiment. Next time you are in
your lathe space fix one little thing from your ToDo list and experience the two-fold benefit of the
fix itself and the relief of not carrying that ToDo
item any more. I think you will be pleasantly
surprised.

➢ Always wear safety goggles or safety glasses that
include side protectors. Use a full face shield for
bowl, vessel, or any turning involving chucks and
faceplates.
➢ Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder
and wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
➢ Wear hearing protection during extended periods
of turning.
➢ Turn the lathe off before adjusting the tool rest or
tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
➢ Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches,
and knockout bars immediately after use. Never
leave them in place, even for a moment.
➢ Tie back long hair and avoid loose clothing, jewelry,
or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating
parts or accessories.
➢ When using a faceplate, be certain the workpiece is
solidly mounted with stout screws (#10 or #12
sheet metal screws as a minimum). Do not use dry
wall or deck screws.
➢ When turning between centers, be certain the
workpiece is firmly mounted between the headstock driving center and tailstock center.
➢ Ensure the belt guard or cover is in place.
➢ Check that all locking devices on the tailstock and
tool rest assembly (rest and base) are tight before
operating the lathe.
➢ Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
➢ Rotate your workpiece backwards by hand to make
sure it clears the toolrest and bed before turning
the lathe on.
➢ Stay clear of the areas directly behind and in front
of the workpiece, they are the most likely areas for
a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good
safety habit is to step out of this zone when turning
on the lathe, keeping your hand on the switch in
case you need to turn the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
➢ Always check the speed of the lathe before turning
it on. Use slower speeds for larger diameters or
rough pieces and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a
piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the
machine to verify why. As a starting point, consult
your operator’s manual for recommended speeds
for a particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed is
compatible with the size of the blank.
➢ Exercise extra caution when using stock with
cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular
shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid
these types of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
➢ Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding
the tool in a controlled but comfortable manner.
Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
➢ Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is
possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless
it is securely tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
➢ Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning turners.
➢ Always remove the tool rest before sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
➢ Don’t overreach, keep proper footing, and keep
your balance at all times.
➢ Keep your lathe in good repair. Check for damaged
parts, alignment, binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect its operation.

The concept is simple. Dismantle your scroll chuck’s jaws/followers – note the followers are labeled 1 – 4 (Fig 1).
Taking #1 & #2 jaws feed them into the scroll as normal. Keep rotating the scroll PAST the #3 & #4 tee-slots and
insert them on the second revolution (Fig 3). Once completed they look like this (Fig 4). You have successfully
configured your chuck into an eccentric one. Mount your jaws. It is mandatory that you use a tall jaw set in order
to have enough axial grip on your blank. For safety, your blank should be no longer than about 5 inches and no
more than 3 inches in diameter. You can use your tail stock for support if you feel the blank needs extra support.
To turn, mount the blank and use a narrow parting tool to remove material until you reach a solid cylinder. Stop!
Then loosen the jaws and advance the blank a set amount. Turn the adjoining cylinder down to solid. Repeat
(Figs 5-7). For the box depicted there were 12 centres( 30 degrees) from one step to the next. Layout is not
shown , but easy to do. You can do this between centres! But, this method is faster!
Be safe! If you are uncomfortable trying this, DON’T!
